item.title: No Picnic on Mount Kenya by Felice Benuzzi (1947)
item.dc:creator: Sophia Jaffer
item.description:
No Picnic on Mount Kenya by Felice Benuzzi (1947)

★★★★

I judged this book by its cover. The bold, lino-esque cover depicts a man dangling from a rockface against a scarlet snow-studded mountain peak. It was a semi-deliberated treat of a buy, one afternoon stroll in Waterstones. I rarely buy books new, a loyal proponent of the charity shop bargain bin. I like to buy books randomly, judging them by their covers and blurbs to discover unknown authors, rather than deliberately chase after safe bets. It’s a risky strategy that certainly doesn’t always work in my favour. For No Picnic on Mount Kenya, it did.

This is a non-fiction book about three Italian Prisoners of War (POWs) who escaped from a British POW Camp near Nanyuki, Kenya in 1943 to reach the summit of Mount Kenya. The three POWs in question, Felice Benuzzi, Dr. Giovanni (‘Giuàn’) Balletto and Vincenzo (‘Enzo’) Barsotti, escaped the camp and summitted Point Lenana with handmade equipment and very meagre rations. They then snuck back into the camp to punishment in solitary confinement. It’s a brilliant story and a mountaineering classic. Benuzzi is not a technically astounding writer, but he does a great job of conveying the bizarre nature of the adventure and the urgency of both the summit and survival of hunger, various threats (animal and human) and the elements. I read most of this book during a trip to Stavanger, Norway, and found myself desperate to climb a mountain as soon as I could. If three amateur Italian POWs could do it with no real equipment, food or shelter, then surely I can?

No Picnic on Mount Kenya is an easy, fascinating read. I went to Kenya myself, in 2017, but not anywhere near this majestic mountain. It is hard to picture just how remote and wild the route was, although Benuzzi tries his best to create an engaging portrayal. Mount Kenya is the second highest mountain in Africa, a volcano created approximately three million years after the opening of the East African Rift. The highest peak, the one that Benuzzi and his companions originally aimed to summit (but ultimately failed due to harsh weather conditions and exhaustion) is Batian, shortly followed by Nelion and then Lenana. One of the best sections of the book is a retrospective addition from Benuzzi detailing the history of Mount Kenya, including those Europeans and Africans who climbed and lived on its great rockfaces. At the time of their summit, the three Italians only had a picture of the south face of Mount Kenya on the label of an Oxo tin. It’s astounding that they managed to summit at all.

I would definitely recommend to anyone who is a fan of mountaineering, or (like me) just admires adventure. Hopefully one day I’ll be writing about my own summit of a mountain peak. Until then, I’ll read books like this one and imagine myself at the base, staring up with wonder at those elusive peaks.

The cover image for this post is a painting with gouache, of some unnamed mountains (although not those found in East Africa).

item.title: Flashlight by Susan Choi (2025)
item.dc:creator: Sophia Jaffer
item.description:
Flashlight by Susan Choi (2025)

★★★★

In the first pages of Susan Choi’s Flashlight, you are sucked into a haunting mystery. Louisa and her father Serk went out for a walk one evening along the sand of a coastal town in Japan. By morning they have failed to return, a search party is commenced, and while Louisa is found unconscious at the breakwater, Serk has disappeared, without trace, into the roaring depths of the ocean. There unravels a generational tale of a small nuclear family unit, traversing from Japan to the US to Korea, and eventually spitting you, the reader, back out of the mystery with the same aggression and force of the tide washing Louisa back to shore.

Flashlight is a history embedded in a work of sweeping literary fiction. Its strengths lie primarily in its exquisite handling of a dark part of Korean history: the abduction of Japanese citizens by the DPRK (Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, or, North Korea) between 1977 and 1983. Serk (born Seok) is a Japanese born ethnic Korean, who emigrates to the US and meets Anne, a wayward youngest daughter of a large American family, who he later marries and moves to Japan with their daughter, Louisa. These characters are complex and often repelling, with fraught relationships and unpredictable, aggressive personalities. Following their move to Japan, and Serk’s subsequent disappearance, Anne and Louisa move back to the US, assuming that Serk has drowned, and continue with their lives. The novel is narrated from multiple third-person perspectives, and through this, we discover that Serk has been abducted by the DPRK and has lived for years in re-education camps in North Korea, eventually escaping to China, where he helped underground organisations to liberate others from North Korea. In the final chapter of the novel, deep in the grips of dementia, Serk is reunited with Louisa as an adult with grown-up children, only a dim recollection of her and the family he lost.

In the 1970s, several disappearances were focused around Japanese coastal areas. The missing were ordinary Japanese citizens, largely in their twenties (although the youngest was just thirteen), many of whom were abducted to teach Japanese language and culture at North Korean spy schools. This is Serk’s fate. He is fed repeated lies about Louisa’s fate and location, tortured and indoctrinated, then ordered to teach Japanese to mysterious young men. The abductions were denied by North Korea, but eventually admitted during talks in 2002, with five abductee victims (and their families) returned. There are several alleged victims still missing. In her account of Serk’s later life in the DPRK, Choi paints a terrifying, desolate picture of the communist dictatorship, where Serk survives on rat meat and scraps. Flashlight is my favourite type of ‘historical’ fiction, which does not advertise its intensions from the cover but instead weaves a historical thread into an otherwise grounded exploration of character and relationships.

I would only fault Flashlight for its ambitious temporal scope, which often leaves the characters in the dust. The lead up to Japan allows for an interesting exploration into Serk, Anne and Louisa, their dynamic as a family and their respective personalities. This collapses after Serk’s disappearance, where events are rushed to accommodate the passage of time, and certain life-altering or traumatic events are dropped without exploration or recognition (the best example of this is Louisa’s assault by British Border Control during her travels as a student). When the objective of the novel is so opaque, it can become obvious that characters are vehicles rather than independent entities. Flashlight certainly does suffer from this at times, and it is the only reason why I would rate it under five stars. There are equally poignant moments, however, that are based on the careful construction of relationships, and it is often Choi’s writing – eloquent, visceral and gorgeous – that allows such an image to form. Flashlight is a transportation to another world – in fact, several worlds – with a competent, creative captain at the helm.

item.title: (Still) Life
item.dc:creator: Sophia Jaffer
item.description:
(Still) Life

I have never been the biggest fan of still life paintings. In my “local” museum, Cambridge’s Fitzwilliam, the first room in the upstairs gallery is a self-proclaimed “Flower Room”, the walls lined from floor to ceiling with technically impeccable depictions of flower vases. I have always liked this room, largely for the overall impression it gives, the way you can lose yourself in the uniformity and simplicity. Take a closer look, however, and I’m almost immediately bored. All the paintings look the same. While their technique and skill are faultless, these painting don’t make me feel very much, and what’s the point of art if it doesn’t make you feel, right?

We painted a lot of still life in school for this very purpose: it develops important skills within a controlled environment, that allows an artist to develop their understanding of several important aspects of painting. As the artist, you set up the composition, meaning that you decide on the light, the objects, the difficulty, as well as creating through the image a narrative, theme or colour harmony. Still life is not a simple snapshot of some objects lying around, it is often carefully orchestrated, it can mean something just as a portrait might. Some still life paintings worth mentioning are Paul Cezanne’s Still Life with Sugar, Caravaggio’s Basket of Fruit, Vincent Van Gogh’s Sunflowers and John Singer Sargent’s Roses. I’ll focus on each in turn. Cezanne’s Still Life carries with it a distinct sense of movement beyond the frame, the tablecloth is rumpled beneath the fruit, the scene feels rushed and quite technically inaccurate in terms of its use of perspective. It is an impression fit for a (post)impressionist. Caravaggio is, in contrast, far more technically accurate. His level of detail is immaculate, if a little harshly defined against the plain background. This reminds me of the flower paintings, although I do feel a twinge of something looking at it, an admiration of the Baroque perfection, perhaps. Sunflowers needs no further introduction. If you were ever to feel something looking at a still life, you would feel it with this. What makes Sunflowers so compelling is not just the fact that we know the artist (as Van Gogh’s own life and history are doubtlessly a powerful emotional pull to his paintings), but it is that we feel as if we truly know the subject. When I look at this painting, I can see the moment it’s captured, the flowers that will doubtlessly shrivel and die beyond the frame, engendering a melancholy beauty to their proud heads. Sargent’s Roses are just a step beyond. The beautifully composed handful of roses lie on the edge of a desk, they are almost decaying before our eyes.

There, then, is the beauty I have found in still life. For a moment, they stop time, they stop decay, they stop life. They exist in a moment where the flower is forever in bloom, the plum always ripe, the apple always browning. All those flowers in the Fitzwilliam died a very long time ago, and every time a curious visitor steps into Gallery 17, they are born again.

The paintings throughout this article are attempts of still life from a holiday in Wales in 2025. They are not technically admirable, rely far more on bold colour and contrast than they do on meaning or vision. They are painted with gouache, each completed within a two-hour period (the time it takes to watch a film) and inspired not by objects before me, but rather hastily found Pinterest pics. They did, however, give me a little taste of still life splendour, provided a drive to try more, to compose my own images, and to depict life even when it’s standing still.
